title: Sent Out: Cyprus and Pisidian Antioch
summary: The Holy Spirit tells the church at Antioch to set apart Barnabas and Saul, and they sail to Cyprus, where the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus believes after Paul confronts a Jewish sorcerer. Crossing to the mainland, they preach in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, where Paul tells Israel's story from the exodus to the resurrection of Jesus. When some Jewish leaders reject the message, Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, many believe, and the missionaries are driven out of the region.
story: Until now the gospel has spread through persecution, scattering, and individual encounters. Here, for the first time, a church deliberately sends people out to carry it to new regions. This begins what readers usually call Paul's first missionary trip (chapters 13 and 14). Two changes signal that a new stage has begun. Saul starts to be called by his Roman name, Paul, and he moves from second place (Barnabas and Saul) to first (Paul and his companions, Paul and Barnabas). The long sermon at Pisidian Antioch is Luke's model of how Paul preached in a synagogue, just as Peter's Pentecost sermon was the model for Jerusalem. And the pattern that will repeat for the rest of the book appears here in full: to the Jew first, then welcome among Gentiles, then opposition and departure.
historical:
Paul's travels can only be dated approximately. The firmest anchor is an inscription found at Delphi in Greece, a letter of the emperor Claudius that dates Gallio's term as proconsul of Achaia to about AD 51-52; Paul appeared before Gallio at Corinth (18:12). Working backward from that point, most scholars place this first trip in the mid to late 40s AD, roughly AD 46 to 48, before the council in Jerusalem.

Cyprus had been a Roman province governed by the Senate since the time of Augustus, and its governor bore the title proconsul, the exact title Luke uses. Salamis, on the east coast, was the island's chief commercial city with a Jewish community large enough for several synagogues; Paphos, on the west coast, was the seat of the governor. Inscriptions mention men named Sergius Paullus, including one in Rome among the officials in charge of the Tiber's banks under Claudius, and some scholars link that family with this proconsul, though the identification is not certain. On the mainland, Perga was a city of Pamphylia on the southern coast, and Pisidian Antioch lay about a hundred miles inland across the Taurus Mountains. It was a Roman colony, settled with veterans by Augustus, and belonged to the large province of Galatia. The road up from the coast was steep and could be dangerous.
cultural:
The service at Pisidian Antioch follows the pattern known from Jewish sources: prayers, a reading from the Law (the five books of Moses), a reading from the Prophets, and then a sermon or word of encouragement from a qualified man, often a visitor. The synagogue leaders (an office attested in inscriptions, including one from Jerusalem) invite Paul to speak. Paul addresses two groups: Men of Israel and the Gentiles who fear God. The God-fearers, along with converts (proselytes, Gentiles who had fully become Jews), were the bridge by which the message reached the wider city.

Bar-Jesus, or Elymas, is a magos, a word that could mean a learned adviser or astrologer or, as here, a practitioner of magic. Educated Romans sometimes kept such figures in their households. The religious women of prominence in verse 50 reflect another feature of the Greek cities of Asia Minor: women of wealthy families often held public influence, and many were attracted to the synagogue. Shaking dust from the feet (verse 51) was a gesture of separation that Jesus had told his disciples to use toward towns that rejected them (Luke 9:5).
literary: The chapter has three parts: the commissioning at Antioch (verses 1-3), the confrontation on Cyprus (verses 4-12), and the long scene at Pisidian Antioch (verses 13-52). Paul's sermon is the centerpiece and falls into three movements, each marked by a fresh address to his hearers. First he retells Israel's history from the exodus to David (verses 16-25), then he proclaims Jesus as the promised son of David, killed and raised (verses 26-37), and finally he calls for a response (verses 38-41). He supports the resurrection with a chain of Old Testament texts: Psalm 2:7, Isaiah 55:3, and Psalm 16:10, linked by the shared ideas of David and of what is holy. The Cyprus scene has an ironic touch: a man named Bar-Jesus, son of Jesus or son of Joshua, opposes the message about Jesus and is struck blind, much as Paul himself once was.

outline.t: The Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul
Cyprus: Elymas blinded and the proconsul believes
Paul's sermon: from the exodus to David and John
Jesus killed and raised, as God promised
Rejection, a turn to the Gentiles, and expulsion

doctrines.note: Paul announces that through Jesus the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed, and that everyone who believes is justified from everything the law of Moses could not justify (verse 39). This is the first statement in Acts in the language that dominates Paul's letters.

Paul applies to himself and Barnabas the words of Isaiah 49:6, where the Lord's servant is made a light for the Gentiles. The church's mission continues the servant's calling: Israel's light was always meant for the ends of the earth.

Luke says that all who were appointed for eternal life believed (verse 48). The line affirms that God's purpose stands behind faith, even as the chapter holds hearers responsible for rejecting the word.
The sermon presents Jesus as the promised descendant of David, the one to whom God said You are My Son. His resurrection is the fulfillment of what God promised our fathers.

words.note: Dikaioo, to justify, to declare or treat someone as in the right. It is a legal word: a judge justifies by pronouncing a verdict. In verse 39 the BSB renders it justified, and it points forward to Paul's argument in Galatians and Romans that God's verdict of acceptance comes through faith in Christ, not by the works of the law.

Tasso, to arrange, appoint, or assign. It is used of soldiers stationed at posts and of people assigned to a task. In verse 48 it describes those appointed for eternal life. Interpreters differ on how much weight the word carries in debates about predestination, as the hard question below explains.

Aphorizo, to set apart or separate. The Spirit says, Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul. Paul later uses the same verb of himself as set apart for the gospel of God (Romans 1:1). Being set apart means being dedicated to a task, not withdrawn from the world.

christ: The sermon at Pisidian Antioch is one of the fullest explanations in Acts of who Jesus is. He is the Savior God brought from the descendants of David, as He promised (verse 23). He was condemned without cause by those who did not recognize him, and in that very act they fulfilled the prophets. He was buried, and God raised Him from the dead, never to see decay. Paul's argument from Psalm 16 is that David died and his body decayed, so the Holy One who would not see decay must be someone else, the son of David whom God raised. Paul also gives Psalm 2's royal decree, You are My Son, a fresh sense: the resurrection is the day God publicly installed Jesus as the Son and King. Through him comes forgiveness and a verdict of righteousness that the law could not supply.

hard.q: Does verse 48 mean that God chose some people for eternal life and not others?
hard.a:
The sentence says that all who were appointed for eternal life believed. Christians in the Reformed or Calvinist tradition read this as a clear statement of election: God appointed certain people to eternal life, and those people believed in response to the word. On this reading faith is the result of God's prior choice, not its cause, and the verse fits Paul's teaching in passages like Ephesians 1:4-5.

Christians in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, and many in Catholic and Orthodox churches, read it differently. Some note that the Greek form of the verb can be read as middle rather than passive, giving something like those who were disposed toward eternal life believed, though most grammarians prefer the passive. Others accept the passive but argue that God's appointing takes account of human response, or refers to God's gracious purpose to save Gentiles as a group, which is the point of the context. Both sides agree on what the chapter holds together: God's purpose stands behind the spread of the gospel, and the hearers who reject it are still addressed as responsible for judging themselves unworthy of eternal life (verse 46). This is a second-order question on which faithful Christians disagree.

questions: The Spirit spoke to the church while its leaders were worshiping and fasting. What does it look like for a church to make decisions that way?
Paul told Israel's story as the setting for Jesus. How does knowing the Old Testament change the way you understand who Jesus is?
The missionaries were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit even as they were driven out of town. Where have you seen joy survive in hard circumstances?
